# Warm-up - plot stickleback data

## Last week's job, two new languages

- You have already piped the stickleback table through `grep`, `sed` and `awk`, and in L03 you ran a first Python script on it.

- Here is that job again - *read the data, total the counts per fish, draw boxplots by group* - as an **R script** and a **Python script** that write the figure to an **SVG file**.

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# Script: plot_stickleback_boxplots.R
# Purpose: boxplots of total RNA-seq counts per group, written to an SVG

infile <- "data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv"              
if (!file.exists(infile)) {
  cat("Error: File", infile, "not found!\n")
  quit(status = 1)
}

stickle <- read.delim(infile, check.names = FALSE)  # keep the name "Geno&Micro"
genes   <- grep("^Gene", names(stickle))            # which columns are genes?
totals  <- rowSums(stickle[, genes])                # one number per fish
group   <- stickle[["Geno&Micro"]]

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
svg("results/total_counts_by_group.svg", width = 7, height = 5)
boxplot(totals ~ group,
        xlab = "Genotype x microbiota group",
        ylab = "Total reads per fish",
        main = "Stickleback gut RNA-seq: total counts by group")
invisible(dev.off())    # close the file device, quietly
cat("Wrote results/total_counts_by_group.svg\n")
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Script: plot_stickleback_boxplots.py
# Purpose: boxplots of total RNA-seq counts per group, written to an SVG

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")                 # draw straight to a file - no window
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

infile = Path("data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv")         
if not infile.is_file():
    print(f"Error: File {infile} not found!")
    sys.exit(1)

stickle = pd.read_csv(infile, sep="\t")
genes   = [c for c in stickle.columns if c.startswith("Gene")]
totals  = pd.DataFrame({
    "Group": stickle["Geno&Micro"],
    "Total": stickle[genes].sum(axis=1),          # one number per fish
})

Path("results").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
totals.boxplot(column="Total", by="Group")
plt.suptitle("")                      # drop pandas' default super-title
plt.title("Stickleback gut RNA-seq: total counts by group")
plt.xlabel("Genotype x microbiota group")
plt.ylabel("Total reads per fish")
plt.savefig("results/total_counts_by_group.svg")  # .svg picks the format
print("Wrote results/total_counts_by_group.svg")
```
:::

:::

## Running R and Python scripts from the shell

::: panel-tabset
### R

``` bash
Rscript plot_stickleback_boxplots.R         # run with the interpreter ...

chmod +x plot_stickleback_boxplots.R        # ... or make it executable
./plot_stickleback_boxplots.R               #     (needs the #!/usr/bin/env Rscript shebang)
```

- `Rscript` runs the file top to bottom and prints only what you `cat()` or `print()`
- In **Positron** / **VS Code**: open the `.R` file and press `Cmd/Ctrl-Enter` to send lines to the console

### Python

``` bash
python3 plot_stickleback_boxplots.py        # run with the interpreter ...

chmod +x plot_stickleback_boxplots.py       # ... or make it executable
./plot_stickleback_boxplots.py              #     (needs the #!/usr/bin/env python3 shebang)
```

- `python3 script.py` runs the file top to bottom and prints only what you `print()`
- In **Positron** / **VS Code**: open the `.py` file and press `Cmd/Ctrl-Enter`, or use the Run button
- Keep project packages in a virtual environment: `python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate` (environments get their full story in L07)
:::

::: callout-tip
- Both languages give a script an **exit status** (`quit(status = 1)` / `sys.exit(1)`), so a shell pipeline or SLURM job can tell whether it succeeded - just like `exit 1` in bash.

- You will write both of these scripts yourself in the finale, and in Lecture 08 we submit them to Talapas inside an `sbatch` job.
:::

# R and Python

## Why use `R`?

- Good general scripting tool for statistics and mathematics
- Powerful and flexible and free
- Runs on all computer platforms
- New enhancements coming out all the time
- Superb data management & graphics capabilities
- Reproducibility - can keep your scripts to see exactly what was done
- You can write your own functions
- Lots of online help available
- Can use a nice IDE such as `Positron`
- Can embed your `R` analyses in dynamic, polished files using `Quarto Markdown`
- Quarto Markdown can be reused for websites, papers, books, presentations...

## Why use `Python`?

- A general-purpose language that is also excellent for data analysis (`pandas`, `numpy`, `matplotlib`, `scipy`)
- The language of machine learning, image analysis and instrument control (`scikit-learn`, `PyTorch`, `scikit-image`)
- Free, open source, runs everywhere - including Talapas (`module load python3`)
- Huge ecosystem: `pip install` gives you access to \>500,000 packages on PyPI; `conda` adds compiled scientific tools
- Readable syntax; indentation *is* the structure of the code
- Runs as scripts (`python3 script.py`), interactively (REPL / IPython), in **Jupyter notebooks**, and in **Quarto** `{python}` chunks
- Same IDE: **Positron** (and **VS Code**) runs R and Python side by side

::: callout-tip
- You do not have to choose. Most computational biologists use **both**:

  - R for statistics and figures

  - Python for pipelines, images and machine learning.

- This lecture shows every idea in both languages - use the tabs.
:::

## R vs Python: same ideas, different syntax

| Idea | R | Python |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Assignment | `x <- 5` | `x = 5` |
| Counting starts at | **1**: `x[1]` is the first element | **0**: `x[0]` is the first element |
| Last element | `x[length(x)]`; `x[-1]` *drops* the first | `x[-1]` *is* the last |
| Sequence of values | vector `c(1, 2, 3)` | list `[1, 2, 3]` or `numpy` array `np.array([1, 2, 3])` |
| Vector arithmetic | `x^2` on any vector | `x**2` only on a numpy array (a list needs a loop) |
| Table of data | `data.frame` / tibble | `pandas` `DataFrame` |
| Load a package | `library(dplyr)` | `import pandas as pd` |
| Install a package | `install.packages("dplyr")` | `pip install pandas` |
| Chain steps | pipe `x |> f() |> g()` | method chaining `x.f().g()` |
| Blocks | curly braces `{ }` | indentation (4 spaces) |
| Missing value | `NA` | `None`, `float("nan")`, `pd.NA` |
| Help | `?mean` | `help(statistics.mean)` or `mean?` in Jupyter |

# R and Python syntax

- Every example in this section and the next two is a runnable cell in the two companion notebooks on the [Examples page](../Examples.html): `Lecture05_R_fundamentals.ipynb` and `Lecture05_Python_fundamentals.ipynb`.

- Download them, open them in Positron, and run along.

- Two topics live *only* in the notebooks - **working with strings** (`paste0`, `sprintf` / f-strings, slicing) and **managing your workspace** (`ls()`, `rm()` / `del`, `%whos`) - so be sure to run those cells too.

## The basics: arithmetic

- Commands can be submitted through the terminal, console or scripts (R: `R` / `Rscript`; Python: `python3` / `python3 script.py`)
- Notice on these slides I'm evaluating the code chunks and showing output
- Also notice that both languages follow the normal priority of mathematical evaluation
- Careful: exponent is `^` in R but `**` in Python (`^` in Python is bitwise XOR!)

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
4*4
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
(4+3*2^2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
4*4
# 16
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
(4+3*2**2)
# 16
```
:::

:::

## Comments, names and style

- Comments start with `#` and run to the end of the line - in bash, R *and* Python
- Both languages are **case sensitive**: `Weight`, `weight` and `WEIGHT` are three different names
- Legal names: letters, digits, `_` (and `.` in R); must not *start* with a digit
- Style: use `snake_case`, short but descriptive - `mean_gc`, `n_fish`, `total_reads`
- Assigning to an existing name silently **overwrites** it - a frequent source of bugs


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# This line is a comment in both languages
n_fish <- 80          # so is everything after the code
n_fish
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 80
```


:::
:::


## Assigning variables

- Assign values with `<-` in R and `=` in Python
- R also accepts `=` for assignment, but course (and community) style is `<-`
- Python can assign several variables at once: `a, b = 1, 2`

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- 2
x*3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
y <- x * 3
y-2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4
```


:::
:::


These do not work


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
3y <- 3
3*y <- 3
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
x = 2
x*3
# 6
y = x * 3
y-2
# 4
a, b = 1, 2          # multiple assignment in one line
```
:::


These do not work either (`SyntaxError`)

``` python
3y = 3
3*y = 3
```
:::

## Arithmetic operations on functions

- Arithmetic operations can be performed easily on functions as well as numbers.
- Try the following, and then your own.

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x+2
x^2
log(x)
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import math

x+2
x**2
math.log(x)
```
:::

:::

- Note that the last of these - `log` - is a built in function of `R`, and therefore the object of the function needs to be put in parentheses
- In Python, `log` lives in the `math` module, so we `import math` once and call `math.log(x)` (`numpy` has `np.log()` for whole arrays)
- These parentheses will be important, and we'll come back to them later when we add arguments after the object in the parentheses\
- The outcome of calculations can be assigned to new variables as well, and the results can be checked using the 'print' command

## Arithmetic operations on functions

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
y <- 67
print(y)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 67
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- 124
z <- (x*y)^2
print(z)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 69022864
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
y = 67
print(y)
# 67

x = 124
z = (x*y)**2
print(z)
# 69022864
```
:::

:::

## Comparisons and logical values

- Comparisons *ask questions* about values and return a **logical** (R) or **bool** (Python) - the foundation of filtering and indexing later today

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- 5
x > 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x == 10          # equality is == (a single = would try to assign!)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x != 10
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(x > 1) & (x < 10)    # AND
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(x < 1) | (x > 4)     # OR
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
!(x > 3)              # NOT
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
x = 5
x > 3
# True
x == 10          # equality is == here too
# False
x != 10
# True
(x > 1) and (x < 10)   # AND is the word "and"
# True
(x < 1) or (x > 4)     # OR is the word "or"
# True
not (x > 3)            # NOT is the word "not"
# False
```
:::

:::

- R spells the logical values `TRUE` / `FALSE`; Python capitalizes only the first letter: `True` / `False`
- R uses the symbols `&`, `|`, `!`; Python uses the *words* `and`, `or`, `not` (the symbols `&` and `|` are reserved for element-wise work on numpy arrays and pandas columns)
- Much more on logical operators and filtering in L07

## STRINGS

- Variables and operations can be performed on characters as well
- Note that characters need to be set off by quotation marks to differentiate them from numbers
- The `c` stands for `concatenate`; in Python square brackets `[ ]` build a **list**
- Note that we are using the same variable names as we did previously, which means that we're overwriting our previous assignment
- A good rule of thumb is to use new names for each variable, and make them short but still descriptive

## STRINGS

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- "I Love"
print (x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "I Love"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
y <- "Bioengineering"
print (y)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Bioengineering"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
z <- c(x,y)
print (z)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "I Love"         "Bioengineering"
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
x = "I Love"
print(x)
# I Love
y = "Bioengineering"
print(y)
# Bioengineering
z = [x, y]
print(z)
# ['I Love', 'Bioengineering']
print(x + " " + y)      # + joins strings
# I Love Bioengineering
```
:::

:::

## VECTORS

- In general `R` thinks in terms of vectors (a list of characters, factors or numerical values).
- It will benefit any `R` user to try to write programs with that in mind, as it will simplify most things.
- Vectors can be assigned directly using the `c()` function and then entering the exact values.
- Python has **lists** (`[ ]`) for any collection, and **numpy arrays** (`np.array()`) when you want R-style vector math
- `x^2` squares every element of an R vector; in Python that only works on a numpy array - a list needs a loop or a *list comprehension*

## VECTORS

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(2,3,4,2,1,2,4,5,10,8,9)
print(x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1]  2  3  4  2  1  2  4  5 10  8  9
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(2,3,4,2,1,2,4,5,10,8,9)
y <- x^2
print(x)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1]  2  3  4  2  1  2  4  5 10  8  9
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
print(y)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1]   4   9  16   4   1   4  16  25 100  64  81
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
x = [2,3,4,2,1,2,4,5,10,8,9]     # a list
print(x)
# [2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 8, 9]
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

x = np.array([2,3,4,2,1,2,4,5,10,8,9])   # a numpy array
y = x**2                                 # element-wise, like R
print(x)
# [ 2  3  4  2  1  2  4  5 10  8  9]
print(y)
# [  4   9  16   4   1   4  16  25 100  64  81]
# with a plain list you would write: y = [v**2 for v in x]
```
:::

:::

## Creating vectors

- Typing vectors in by hand is a drag - use generating functions instead: `seq()` and `rep()` in R; `range()`, `np.arange()`, `np.linspace()` in Python
- Try the examples and vary the arguments - can you work out what each one does?

### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

seq_1 = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, 101)    # 101 points from 0 to 10 (step 0.1)
print(seq_1)
# [ 0.   0.1  0.2 ...  9.8  9.9 10. ]
seq_2 = np.linspace(10.0, 0.0, 101)

seq_square     = seq_2 * seq_2         # element-wise ...
seq_square_new = seq_2**2              # ... same result
print(seq_square_new)
# [100.    98.01  96.04 ...   0.04   0.01   0.  ]

list(range(10))                        # integers 0, 1, ..., 9 (start defaults to 0; stop excluded!)
np.tile(["A", "B"], 3)                 # like rep(..., times = 3)
# ['A' 'B' 'A' 'B' 'A' 'B']
np.repeat(["A", "B"], 3)               # like rep(..., each = 3)
# ['A' 'A' 'A' 'B' 'B' 'B']
```
:::

:::

## Basic Statistics

- Many functions exist to operate on vectors.
- Combine these with your previous variable to see what happens.
- Also, try to find other functions (e.g. standard deviation).

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(x)
median(x)
var(x)
log(x)  # natural log
sqrt(x)
sum(x)
length(x)
sample(x, replace = TRUE)
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

x.mean()                     # or np.mean(x)
np.median(x)
x.var(ddof=1)                # sample variance, like R's var()
np.log(x)                    # natural log, element-wise
np.sqrt(x)
x.sum()                      # sum(x) also works
len(x)                       # length(x)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)         # a seeded random generator (like set.seed)
rng.choice(x, size=len(x), replace=True)  # sample with replacement
```
:::

:::

- Notice that the last function (`sample`) has an argument (`replace=T`); in Python the generator's `rng.choice()` samples *with* replacement when `replace=True`, and `size=` sets how many - the same `default_rng()` generator powers all the random sampling in L06
- Python functions come in two flavours: `np.median(x)` (function) and `x.mean()` (a **method** attached to the array)
- Arguments simply modify or direct the function in some way
- There are many arguments for each function, some of which are defaults

# Data types in R and Python

## Scales of measurement

| Scale | What it is | Example | Typical computer type |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| **Nominal** (categorical) | Unordered labels | genotype A / B; apples, oranges | character or factor |
| **Ordinal** (categorical) | Ordered labels | small \< medium \< large | ordered factor |
| **Discrete** (quantitative) | Whole-number counts | RNA-seq reads per gene | integer |
| **Continuous** (quantitative) | Measurements | mass (kg), length (mm) | double / float |

- Among continuous scales:
  - a **ratio** scale has a true zero (mass, length, counts);
  - an **interval** scale does not (temperature in °C, calendar year)
- `Factor` is R's special type for categorical variables - we will explore it more later

## The same types, two sets of names

| What it holds | R (tibble code) | Python | Example |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| TRUE / FALSE | logical (`lgl`) | `bool` | `TRUE` / `True` |
| Whole numbers | integer (`int`) | `int` | `3L` / `3` |
| Real numbers | double (`dbl`) | `float` | `3.0`, `2.5e-3` |
| Text | character (`chr`) | `str` | `"low"` |
| Categories | factor (`fctr`) | `pandas.Categorical` | `factor(c("low","high"))` |
| Dates / date-times | `date` / `dttm` | `datetime.date` / `datetime.datetime` | `as.Date("2026-11-09")` |

- Integer and double vectors are known collectively as **numeric** vectors; in `R` numbers are doubles by default
- Python keeps `int` and `float` strictly apart:
  - `7 / 2` is `3.5` (always a float)
  - `7 // 2` is `3` (integer division)
  - `7 % 2` is the remainder `1`
- R's integer division and remainder are `%/%` and `%%`


- A numpy array or pandas column has one **dtype** shared by every value - just like an R vector

## Converting between types

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
as.numeric("3.14")      # string to number
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3.14
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.character(3.14)      # number to string
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "3.14"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.integer(3.99)        # truncates toward zero - does NOT round
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
as.numeric("abc")       # fails *quietly*: NA plus a warning
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] NA
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
float("3.14")           # string to number
# 3.14
str(3.14)               # number to string
# '3.14'
int(3.99)               # truncates toward zero - does NOT round
# 3
float("abc")            # fails *loudly*: ValueError and the script stops
# ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'abc'
```
:::

:::

- The two languages fail differently:
  - R converts the unconvertible to `NA` with a warning and keeps going
  - Python raises an error and stops
- Both behaviors bite: check for `NA` after converting in R; wrap risky conversions in `try`/`except` in Python (L07)

## One type per vector: coercion

- An R vector holds exactly **one** type - mix types and R silently *coerces* everything to the most flexible one: logical → integer → double → character

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(1, 2, 3)            # double
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1 2 3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
c(1, 2, "three")      # one string turns ALL of them into strings
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "1"     "2"     "three"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
c(1, 2, TRUE)         # TRUE quietly becomes 1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1 2 1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))   # ... which is genuinely useful: counting!
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
[1, 2, "three"]            # a list happily mixes types - no coercion
# [1, 2, 'three']
import numpy as np
np.array([1, 2, "three"])  # a numpy array coerces, just like R
# array(['1', '2', 'three'], dtype='<U21')
sum([True, True, False, True])   # True counts as 1 here too
# 3
```
:::

:::

- Watch for this when reading data: one stray character in a column of numbers turns the **whole column** into strings
- A pandas column that mixes types gets dtype `object` - slow and error-prone; the fix is cleaning the data, not ignoring it

## Special values: missing, impossible and infinite

| Meaning                   | R             | Python / pandas           |
|:--------------------------|:--------------|:--------------------------|
| Missing value             | `NA`          | `None`, `np.nan`, `pd.NA` |
| Not a number (e.g. `0/0`) | `NaN`         | `float("nan")`, `np.nan`  |
| Infinity (e.g. `1/0`)     | `Inf`, `-Inf` | `math.inf`, `np.inf`      |
| No object at all          | `NULL`        | `None`                    |

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
is.na(x)                # never test with == NA  (the answer would be NA!)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(x)                 # one NA poisons the result ...
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] NA
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)   # ... unless you ask to remove it
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.333333
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

x = pd.Series([1, 2, np.nan, 4])
x.isna()                 # like is.na() - never test with == nan
# 0 False, 1 False, 2 True, 3 False
x.mean()                 # pandas SKIPS missing values by default!
# 2.3333...
x.mean(skipna=False)     # ask for R-like behavior
# nan
```
:::

:::

- Logical vectors can take exactly three values: `TRUE`, `FALSE` and `NA`; doubles add `NaN`, `Inf` and `-Inf`
- Mind the opposite defaults: R *keeps* `NA` unless you say `na.rm = TRUE`; pandas *skips* missing values unless you say `skipna=False`

## Beyond vectors: lists and dictionaries

- A vector or array holds many values of **one** type; a **list** (R) or **dictionary** (Python) holds *anything*, with a name for each element

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

fish$mass_g            # elements by name with $ ...
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.42
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fish[["counts"]]       # ... or with [[ ]]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16 15 71
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str(fish)              # names, types and sizes at a glance
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
List of 3
 $ id    : chr "AC1"
 $ mass_g: num 1.42
 $ counts: num [1:3] 16 15 71
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}

fish["mass_g"]         # elements by key
# 1.42
fish.keys()
# dict_keys(['id', 'mass_g', 'counts'])
fish["counts"][0]      # containers nest: the list inside the dict
# 16
```

- Why this matters next: a **data frame is a list of equal-length vectors** - one name per column, one type per column; pandas builds a `DataFrame` from a dictionary of columns the same way
- Python also has **tuples** (`(1, 2)`, immutable) and **sets** (`{1, 2}`, unique values) - Parisa's `s5` and `s6` notebooks work through all four

# Indexing

## Indexing vectors and lists

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- c(2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 8, 9)
x[1]            # the FIRST element - R counts from 1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x[c(1, 3)]      # elements 1 and 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2 4
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x[2:4]          # elements 2 through 4 (both ends included)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3 4 2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x[-1]           # everything EXCEPT element 1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1]  3  4  2  1  2  4  5 10  8  9
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
x[x > 4]        # logical indexing: elements where the condition is TRUE
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  5 10  8  9
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 8, 9])
x[0]            # the FIRST element - Python counts from 0
# 2
x[[0, 2]]       # elements at positions 0 and 2
# [2 4]
x[1:4]          # positions 1, 2, 3 - the stop position is EXCLUDED
# [3 4 2]
x[-1]           # the LAST element (negative = count from the end)
# 9
x[x > 4]        # logical (boolean) indexing, exactly like R
# [ 5 10  8  9]
```
:::

:::

- The same `[ ]` syntax, two opposite conventions: R is **1-based and inclusive**, Python is **0-based and stop-excluded**
- Negative numbers *drop* elements in R but *count from the end* in Python - the classic cross-language bug
- **Logical indexing** (`x[x > 4]`) is identical in both - and it is the idea behind filtering tables, next


## Indexing a data set: rows and single cells

Both languages use `table[row, column]` - the differences are the starting number and labels vs positions:

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

```

```

1        AC1        A
2        AC2        A
3        AC3        A
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}

```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "A"
```


:::


:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
stickle.iloc[0, 0:4]       # first row, first four columns - by POSITION (0-based)
stickle.loc[0:2, ["Individual", "Genotype"]]   # by LABEL (row labels here are 0,1,2)
stickle.loc[2, "Genotype"]     # one single cell: row label 2, column "Genotype"
# 'A'
stickle.iloc[2, 1]             # the same cell, by position
# 'A'
```

- R has one bracket for both jobs; pandas splits them: **`.loc[ ]`** for *labels*, **`.iloc[ ]`** for *positions*

## Reading tabular data

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# comma-separated:   read.csv("file.csv")
# tab-separated:     read.delim("file.tsv")
stickle <- read.delim("../Data_Folder/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv",
                      header = TRUE,          # first line is column names (default)
                      check.names = FALSE)    # keep "Geno&Micro" exactly as written
dim(stickle)      # rows, columns
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  80 604
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stickle[1:2, 1:5]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  Individual Genotype   Microbiota Geno&Micro Gene1
1        AC1        A conventional      convA    16
2        AC2        A conventional      convA     7
```


:::
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd

# pd.read_csv handles both - sep="\t" makes it tab-separated
stickle = pd.read_csv("../Data_Folder/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv", sep="\t")
stickle.shape     # (rows, columns)
# (80, 604)
stickle.iloc[0:2, 0:5]

# pandas reads URLs directly - handy for course data:
# stickle = pd.read_csv("https://wcresko.github.io/BioE_Comp_Tools_Fa2026/Data_Folder/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv", sep="\t")
```

:::

- The two questions every reader function asks: *where are the column names?* (`header`) and *what separates the values?* (`sep`)
- Without `check.names = FALSE`, R "fixes" `Geno&Micro` to `Geno.Micro` - fine, until your column names no longer match the file
- The tidyverse's `readr` (`read_tsv()`, faster and friendlier) takes over in L06

## Writing tabular data

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
totals <- data.frame(Individual = stickle$Individual,
                     Total = rowSums(stickle[, grep("^Gene", names(stickle))]))

write.csv(totals, "results/totals.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.table(totals, "results/totals.tsv", sep = "\t",
            row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE)
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
genes  = [c for c in stickle.columns if c.startswith("Gene")]
totals = pd.DataFrame({"Individual": stickle["Individual"],
                       "Total": stickle[genes].sum(axis=1)})

totals.to_csv("results/totals.csv", index=False)
totals.to_csv("results/totals.tsv", sep="\t", index=False)
```
:::

:::

- `row.names = FALSE` / `index=False` - otherwise both languages sneak an extra unnamed column of row numbers into your file
- Write **derived** tables into `results/` or `output/`; never overwrite anything in `data/` (raw data is read-only - the L01 project structure exists for exactly this reason)

## What can you read and write?

| Format | R | Python |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| CSV / TSV (plain text) | `read.csv()` / `write.csv()` | `pd.read_csv()` / `.to_csv()` |
| Excel `.xlsx` | `readxl::read_excel()` / `writexl` | `pd.read_excel()` / `.to_excel()` |
| Plain text, line by line | `readLines()` / `writeLines()` | `Path.read_text()`, `open()` |
| JSON | `jsonlite::fromJSON()` | `json.load()`, `pd.read_json()` |
| Native binary objects | `saveRDS()` / `readRDS()` | `pickle` |
| Big columnar data | `arrow::read_parquet()` | `pd.read_parquet()` |

- **Plain-text formats (CSV/TSV) are the default**: portable, future-proof, readable by `grep`/`awk`, and diff-able in Git
- Binary formats (`.rds`, `.pickle`, `.parquet`) are faster and preserve types exactly - but only their own language (or ecosystem) can read them
- Excel files are for *exchanging with humans*; convert to CSV/TSV before analysis when you can (remember the gene-name-to-date horror stories)

## Reading and writing in a script

The warm-up scripts already showed the whole pattern - here it is as a checklist:

``` r
infile <- "data/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv"        # 1. relative path from the project root
if (!file.exists(infile)) {                # 2. check before reading,
  cat("Error: File", infile, "not found!\n")
  quit(status = 1)                         #    fail loudly with an exit status
}
stickle <- read.delim(infile, check.names = FALSE)   # 3. read
# ... compute ...
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)          # 4. make the output folder
write.csv(totals, "results/totals.csv", row.names = FALSE)  # 5. write results
```

- **Relative paths** from the project root (`data/...`, `results/...`) - never `/Users/yourname/...`, which breaks on every other machine (including Talapas)
- Python's version of each step: `Path("data/f.tsv")`, `.is_file()`, `sys.exit(1)`, `Path("results").mkdir(exist_ok=True)`, `.to_csv()`
- Run scripts **from the project root** so the relative paths resolve

## Saving figures to files

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
svg("results/boxplot.svg", width = 7, height = 5)   # open a file 'device'
boxplot(totals ~ group)                             # draw into it
dev.off()                                           # close it - ALWAYS

png("results/boxplot.png", width = 7, height = 5,
    units = "in", res = 300)                        # raster needs a resolution
boxplot(totals ~ group)
dev.off()

# pdf("results/boxplot.pdf", ...) works the same way
# ggplot figures: ggsave("results/boxplot.svg") - coming in L07
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.boxplot([1, 2, 3])                 # draw ...
plt.savefig("results/boxplot.svg")     # ... the extension picks the format
plt.savefig("results/boxplot.png", dpi=300)   # raster needs a resolution
plt.savefig("results/boxplot.pdf")
```
:::

:::

- **Vector** formats (`.svg`, `.pdf`) scale forever - use them for papers and posters; **raster** formats (`.png`, 300 dpi) for slides and the web
- R's pattern is *open device → plot → `dev.off()`* (forget `dev.off()` and the file is empty or locked); matplotlib's is simply `plt.savefig()`

# `grep` and regular expressions in R and Python

## The same patterns, new functions

| Job | Shell (L04) | R | Python (`import re`) |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| Which elements match? | `grep` | `grepl()` (TRUE/FALSE), `grep()` (positions) | `re.search()` |
| Pull out the match | `grep -o` | `regmatches()` + `gregexpr()` | `re.findall()` |
| Substitute | `sed 's/a/b/'` | `sub()` (first), `gsub()` (all) | `re.sub()` |
| Split on a pattern | `awk -F` | `strsplit()` | `re.split()` |

- The **patterns themselves are the same** ones you learned in L04: `^` start, `$` end, `[ACGT]` classes, `{3}` counts, `( | )` alternatives
- Two escaping dialects:
  - R needs a double backslash (`"\\d"` for a digit)
  - Python uses **raw strings** (`r"\d"`) - always write Python patterns with the `r` prefix
- The tidyverse's `stringr` (`str_detect()`, `str_replace()`, ...) wraps R's functions with consistent names

::: panel-tabset
### R


```

```

```{.r .cell-code}

```


:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import re
[c for c in stickle.columns if re.search(r"^Gene", c)][:3]  # gene columns
# ['Gene1', 'Gene2', 'Gene3']
stickle["Individual"][stickle["Individual"].str.contains(r"1$")]
# the pandas .str methods apply a regex down a whole column
[re.sub(r"^Gene", "G", c) for c in stickle.columns[4:8]]
# ['G1', 'G2', 'G3', 'G4']
re.split(r"", "convA")       # and re.findall(r"[A-Z]", "convA") pulls out ['A']
```

- `grepl()` on `names(stickle)` is exactly how the warm-up script found the 600 gene columns
- In pandas, the `.str` accessor (`.str.contains()`, `.str.replace()`, `.str.extract()`) runs a regex down an entire column at once

## The L04  `fasta_stats` bash script in R and Python

::: panel-tabset
### R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#!/usr/bin/env Rscript
# Script: fasta_stats.R
# Purpose: Calculate basic statistics for a FASTA file

args <- commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)     # like $1 $2 ... in bash
if (length(args) != 1) {
  cat("Usage: Rscript fasta_stats.R sequences.fasta\n")
  quit(status = 1)
}
input <- args[1]
if (!file.exists(input)) {
  cat("Error: File", input, "not found!\n")
  quit(status = 1)
}

lines   <- readLines(input)
headers <- grepl("^>", lines)                # TRUE for header lines
seq     <- paste(lines[!headers], collapse = "")

cat("=== FASTA Statistics for", input, "===\n")
cat("Number of sequences:", sum(headers), "\n")
cat("Total length:", nchar(seq), "bp\n")
cat("Average length:", nchar(seq) / sum(headers), "bp\n")
n_count <- sum(strsplit(seq, "")[[1]] %in% c("N", "n"))
cat("N bases:", n_count, "\n")
gc <- sum(strsplit(toupper(seq), "")[[1]] %in% c("G", "C"))
cat("GC content:", round(100 * gc / nchar(seq), 1), "%\n")
orfs <- regmatches(seq, gregexpr("ATG([ACGT]{3}){20,}(TAA|TAG|TGA)", seq))[[1]]
cat("ORF-like stretches:", length(orfs), "\n")
```
:::


### Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Script: fasta_stats.py
# Purpose: Calculate basic statistics for a FASTA file

import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

if len(sys.argv) != 2:                       # sys.argv[0] is the script name, like $0
    print("Usage: python3 fasta_stats.py sequences.fasta")
    sys.exit(1)
input_file = Path(sys.argv[1])
if not input_file.is_file():
    print(f"Error: File {input_file} not found!")
    sys.exit(1)

lines   = input_file.read_text().splitlines()
headers = [line for line in lines if line.startswith(">")]
seq     = "".join(line for line in lines if not line.startswith(">"))

print(f"=== FASTA Statistics for {input_file} ===")
print(f"Number of sequences: {len(headers)}")
print(f"Total length: {len(seq)} bp")
print(f"Average length: {len(seq) / len(headers):.1f} bp")
n_count = seq.count("N") + seq.count("n")
print(f"N bases: {n_count}")
gc = seq.upper().count("G") + seq.upper().count("C")
print(f"GC content: {100 * gc / len(seq):.1f}%")
orfs = re.findall(r"ATG(?:[ACGT]{3}){20,}(?:TAA|TAG|TGA)", seq)
print(f"ORF-like stretches: {len(orfs)}")
```
:::

# Finale: write your own executable R and Python scripts

## Anatomy of an executable script

| Ingredient | bash (L02-L04) | R | Python |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| Shebang (line 1) | `#!/bin/bash` | `#!/usr/bin/env Rscript` | `#!/usr/bin/env python3` |
| Make it executable | `chmod +x name.sh` | `chmod +x name.R` | `chmod +x name.py` |
| Run it | `./name.sh` | `./name.R` (or `Rscript name.R`) | `./name.py` (or `python3 name.py`) |
| Arguments | `$1`, `$2` | `commandArgs(trailingOnly = TRUE)` | `sys.argv[1:]` |
| Print | `echo` | `cat()` | `print()` |
| Fail loudly | `exit 1` | `quit(status = 1)` | `sys.exit(1)` |

- The shell does not care what language is inside - the **shebang** tells it which interpreter to hand the file to
- That is why these scripts drop into any pipeline, `cron` job or `sbatch` submission exactly like your week-2 shell scripts

## Summary

- **R and Python share the ideas** - variables, vectors, types, indexing, files - and differ in spelling: `<-` vs `=`, `^` vs `**`, 1-based vs 0-based, `TRUE` vs `True`
- A **script** is a text file plus a shebang, `chmod +x`, arguments and an exit status - in any language
- Every vector/column has **one type**; know `class()` / `type()`, convert deliberately, and respect `NA` / `NaN` (and the opposite `na.rm` / `skipna` defaults)
- **Indexing**: `x[i]`, `table[row, col]`, `$` / `[[ ]]`, `.loc` / `.iloc` - and logical tests select rows like `grep` selects lines
- **Files**: read with `read.delim()` / `pd.read_csv()`, write results (never raw data!), save figures as vector SVG/PDF
- **Regular expressions** moved with you: the L04 patterns now run inside `grepl()` / `gsub()` and `re.findall()` / `re.sub()`
- Next week (L06): data frames in earnest - distributions, summaries and real figures from the stickleback table

  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {

    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {

        }

    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
